lead: A mass transfer coefficient depends on velocity, length, density, viscosity and diffusivity. Measuring it for every fluid and speed is hopeless. So we pack those variables into three dimensionless numbers — Sherwood, Reynolds and Schmidt — and fit one curve through many experiments. Feed in Re and Sc, read out Sh, then convert to k_c.
prereq: You need Chapter 2.1 for k_c, and the Reynolds number and boundary layer from fluid mechanics.

blocks.text: At the surface the flux is still diffusive, N_A = k_c Δc, but stirring steepens the concentration gradient near the wall and so raises k_c. Compare this with the purely diffusive flux D_AB Δc/L over the same length; the ratio is the Sherwood number.

blocks.where: Sh is the Sherwood number (dimensionless), k_c the mass transfer coefficient in m/s, L the characteristic length in m, D_AB the diffusivity of A in B in m²/s.

blocks.text: Reynolds number compares inertia with viscous force and decides whether the boundary layer is laminar or turbulent. Schmidt number compares momentum spreading with mass spreading.
Re = ρ u L / μ = u L / ν      Sc = μ / (ρ D_AB) = ν / D_AB
blocks.where: ρ is density in kg/m³, u the free-stream velocity in m/s, μ the viscosity in Pa·s, ν = μ/ρ the kinematic viscosity in m²/s.

blocks.text: Sh does in mass transfer what Nu = hL/k does in heat transfer, and Sc is the mass version of the Prandtl number. Every correlation therefore reads Sh as a function of Re and Sc.
Steady laminar flow over a flat plate of length L, with Re below about 5×10⁵, gives an average coefficient:

blocks.where: averaged over the plate length L, with Re = uL/ν and u the free-stream velocity.

blocks.text: Turbulent from the leading edge on the same plate:

blocks.where: valid roughly from Re = 5×10⁵ to 10⁷; L is the plate length from the leading edge.

blocks.text: A real plate is laminar near the nose and turbulent further on. That mixed plate needs the 871 correction:

blocks.where: the same plate and the same L; the 871 is the laminar stretch subtracted out, not a term to add.

blocks.text: For a single sphere of diameter d in a flowing stream:

blocks.where: L = d. At Re = 0 it returns Sh = 2, pure diffusion to a sphere in still fluid.

blocks.text: The first two are boundary-layer fits for a flat plate; the sphere fit is an empirical correlation for a different geometry, which is why it carries the additive 2. Sc^(1/3) appears in all three because the laminar sublayer near the surface controls the mass transfer resistance in each case.
Each correlation fixes its own length and its own property temperature. Check both before substituting anything.

items: Pick the geometry: flat plate or single sphere.
Set L in metres: plate length along the flow, or sphere diameter.
Evaluate ρ, μ and D_AB at the film temperature T_f = (T_s + T_∞)/2.
Compute ν = μ/ρ, then Re = uL/ν and Sc = ν/D_AB.
Choose the correlation whose Re range contains your Re; compute Sh.
Convert back: k_c = Sh D_AB / L, in m/s.

blocks.text: For gases Sc usually lies between about 0.2 and 3, near 0.6 for water vapour in air; in liquids Sc reaches hundreds or thousands. Outside the tested Re band a correlation is extrapolation, not prediction. Two correlations may share the algebra but not the length: compare definitions, never symbols.

figure.caption: Sherwood number against Reynolds number at Sc = 0.577. Each line is drawn only over its fitted band: laminar up to Re ≈ 5×10⁵, turbulent from Re ≈ 5×10⁵ upward. The marked point is the worked example, on the laminar line.

spec.aria: Sherwood number against Reynolds number. The laminar line is drawn to Re about 5×10⁵, the turbulent line from there upward, and the worked example point lies on the laminar line.

examples.question: Air at 2 m/s flows over a flat plate 0.5 m long, with D_AB = 2.6×10⁻⁵ m²/s and ν = 1.5×10⁻⁵ m²/s. Use Sh = 0.664 Re^(1/2) Sc^(1/3) to find Re, Sc, Sh and k_c.
steps: Re = uL/ν = (2 × 0.5)/(1.5×10⁻⁵) = 6.67×10⁴. Below 5×10⁵, so the laminar fit applies.
examples.check:
import math
u = 2.0
L = 0.5
D = 2.6e-5
nu = 1.5e-5
Re = u*L/nu
Sc = nu/D
Sh = 0.664*math.sqrt(Re)*Sc**(1/3)
kc = Sh*D/L
print(round(Re, -2))
print(round(Sc, 3))
print(round(Sh, 1))
print(round(kc, 5))

traps: Using plate length for a sphere or diameter for a plate. Each correlation defines its own L; a wrong L spoils Re and k_c together.
Evaluating μ and D_AB at the wall or bulk temperature instead of the film temperature T_f.

Treating Sh = 0.037 Re^0.8 Sc^(1/3) as a whole-plate average. It assumes turbulence from the leading edge; a plate that starts laminar needs Sh = (0.037 Re^0.8 − 871) Sc^(1/3). The correction is a subtraction, not an added laminar term.
Swapping Sh with Nu, or Sc with Pr. The algebra is identical, the symbols are not, and the definition is the first thing marked.

quiz.q: Define Sh and Sc, and give the unit of every symbol in them.
quiz.a: Sh = k_c L/D_AB, dimensionless; Sc = μ/(ρD_AB), dimensionless. k_c in m/s, L in m, D_AB in m²/s, μ in Pa·s, ρ in kg/m³.

quiz.q: Why does every correlation here carry the factor Sc^(1/3)?
quiz.a: The concentration and velocity boundary layers have thicknesses in the ratio Sc^(−1/3); that factor carries the ratio into Sh.

quiz.q: Why are properties evaluated at the film temperature?
quiz.a: Properties vary across the boundary layer; the mean of wall and bulk, T_f = (T_s + T_∞)/2, is the single value the fit was built on.

quiz.q: A 10 mm sphere moves at 0.05 m/s in water with ν = 1.0×10⁻⁶ m²/s and D_AB = 1.0×10⁻⁹ m²/s. Find Re, Sc and Sh.
In the worked example, what happens to Sh and k_c if the velocity doubles?
Two correlations give Sh = 60 and Sh = 900 at the same Re. Give two possible reasons and say how you would choose.
quiz.a: Different geometry or length definition, or a different flow regime (laminar against turbulent). Choose by matching geometry, L definition, Re range and property temperature to your own problem.

beyond: Not for the exam. Rating software stores these fits as tables of j_D = Sh/(Re Sc^(1/3)) against Re, so mass transfer sits beside pressure drop in one database. Research pushes the same idea into microchannels and membrane modules, where Sc runs into the thousands.
